headline: SFPD drone footage accidentally livestreamed for 48 hours, exposing arrests & surveillance
summary: Two security researchers discovered that real-time video, thermal imaging, location data, and pilot details from five San Francisco Police Department surveillance drones were publicly accessible online for 48 hours.
details: For 48 hours last month, the San Francisco Police Department (SFPD) accidentally livestreamed real-time footage from five of its surveillance drones onto the open internet. This included sensitive video of arrests, thermal imaging, location metadata, and even the drone pilots' names and email addresses.

The exposed footage captured a police chase involving a Skydio X10 quadcopter tracking a suspect's SUV across the city. Multiple drones were used to follow the individual, ultimately leading to officers tackling him in response to an alleged "auto boost/strip" incident.

The accidental livestream occurred via drone manufacturer Skydio's website. Security researchers Sam Curry and Maik Robert discovered the public web address where the videos were hosted and reported it to Skydio, after which the feed was quickly taken offline.

During the period the feed was live, the researchers observed police carrying out multiple detentions, apartment visits, and searches, as well as tracking numerous cars and individuals from the sky. This exposure raises significant privacy concerns, as Curry noted, "When you're watching a drone feed live, you can look into dozens of different apartments."

The archive captured by Curry and Robert details SFPD drone operations over approximately 48 hours in mid-June. It comprises 60 videos from 20 separate flights, each recorded from three feeds: a color camera, a thermal camera, and a view from the drone's rooftop dock. Analysis revealed cameras filmed hundreds of people and vehicles.

headline_marked: [[EU plans new social media limits]] for teens across Europe, including age bans
headline: EU plans new social media limits for teens across Europe, including age bans
summary: The European Union is considering sweeping new restrictions on children's and teenagers' access to social media, including age limits, outright bans, and phased access.
details: The European Union is weighing significant new restrictions on children's and teenagers' access to social media platforms. These proposals include age limits, outright bans for very young children, and phased access for older teens.

Social media companies could also be forced to prove their services are not harmful before young people are allowed to use them. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen stated that the bloc's executive arm could propose new legislation within months.

An expert panel recommended a phased approach: "no screens at all" for children under 3, supervised internet use for those under 13, and some limits for older teens. Von der Leyen supports the idea that platforms should have to demonstrate their services are safe for younger users.

The Commission will consider the report and return with formal proposals "after the summer." Any legislation would require approval from the European Parliament and the EU's 27 member countries to become law across the bloc.

These new rules would add significant pressure on platforms to demonstrate their services are safe. The EU has already found Meta in breach of its Digital Services Act over the "addictive" design of Facebook and Instagram, with a similar finding against TikTok earlier this year.
